title: FBC: Firebreak
summary: Leading UI/UX for a co-op multiplayer game, from the first wireframes in preproduction to post-launch support.

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Me and a UI artist, with 3 UI programmers

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Information architecture, flows, HUD, menus, visual style, production planning

meta.label: Tools
meta.value: Figma, Claude AI, Photoshop, After Effects, JS/HTML/CSS, Jira, Confluence, pen and paper

hero.alt: FBC: Firebreak main menu inside a 3D environment

sections.heading: A full game UI, owned by a team of two
body: I joined FBC: Firebreak in preproduction as the lead UI/UX designer. A UI artist and I were the entire design side of the UI, working day to day with a three-person UI programming team.
Beyond the interface, I worked with art direction, the game director, game design, audio and VFX, and helped shape mission design and the core gameplay loop.

sections.heading: Cognitive overload, on a tight schedule
body: A multiplayer game needs far more UI than its gameplay suggests: onboarding, a metagame, loadouts, cosmetics, matchmaking, parties and a HUD that reads under pressure. All of it had to ship together, on a schedule that left little room for rework.

The hardest part was the HUD. Every new feature asked for its own feedback on screen, and in the middle of a co-op fight it piled up. Playtests pointed the same way: most issues came from a gameplay loop that felt confusing, and from UI requests that made the game look more complex than it was.
sections.pull: Not too big, not too small. Not too flashy, not completely mute.

media.alt: In-game HUD during an anomaly interaction
media.caption: In-game HUD

sections.heading: Less HUD, clearer goals
body: I pushed back on game design when feedback didn't earn its place. Where players needed to know something, I looked for diegetic ways to show it in the world.
What stayed on screen was a balancing act between readable and intrusive. For the confusing loop, I pushed for a simple mission tracker that always makes the player's next big goal clear.

media.alt: In-game HUD in a frost anomaly mission
media.caption: HUD in a live mission

sections.heading: Own the structure and the plan
body: I owned the UI end to end: structure, flows, HUD, menus and overall visual style. I also owned the plan. The producer ran the meetings, but the UI programming lead and I built the schedule together in Jira, sprint by sprint and screen by screen.

We started development on screens that were safe to build early, and grouped screens that shared components so each piece was built once and reused. That kept the short- and long-term timeline realistic.

sections.heading: A main menu that lives in the world
body: With the art director, I designed Remedy's first main menu set inside a 3D environment. Nobody at the studio had built one before, so the idea met early pushback. I worked out the technical approach that made it possible.

The point wasn't spectacle. The player's state no longer lived only in the UI but in the game world: pick a loadout and you watch the actual game meshes change on the table in front of you. Each menu item has its own corner of the space and the camera glides there on selection. The setup also opened the door to seasonal and event environments.
sections.pull: Your loadout isn't a list in a menu. It's the gear on the table in front of you.

media.alt: Loadout selection in the 3D menu space
media.caption: Loadout, shown on the table in the 3D menu

sections.heading: Modular flows instead of waiting screens
body: I designed onboarding for the metagame and made matchmaking and the into-game flow fully modular. Players can sit in a queue while still browsing and swapping equipment and cosmetics, instead of staring at a spinner.

sections.heading: Shipped complete and functional
body: The game didn't find the commercial success we hoped for, and we didn't hit every goal we set for the craft team. But on a very tight schedule, the team shipped a complete, polished and functional UI, and I'm proud of what we built together.

sections.heading: What I'd do differently
body: This was my first time leading a project of this scale. More than once I had a gut feeling that a proposed feature or change wouldn't work, and let it through anyway. Next time I'd trust that expertise sooner, push back harder on requests from design and direction, say no when the answer is no, and push for the design I feel would work the best.
